newsitem.title: USA: Changes made in Clinton's education tax proposals.
newsitem.headline: Changes made in Clinton's education tax proposals.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday proposed changes in education initiatives that would make college tax credits available to more people and eliminate a B-minus average grade qualification.
President Clinton's education proposal, especially the grade requirement, had been criticized by members of Congress from both sides of the aisle and the higher education community.

Criticism stemmed from how the HOPE scholarship $1,500 tax credit would be administered if a B-minus average was required. Concerns were expressed about how the Internal Revenue Service would know the grade point average and whether it would lead to grade inflation by educators so students would not lose the tax credit.

The budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the president last month said "roughly" $35 billion of the $135 billion total tax cut package over five years would go toward the president's education proposals.

The higher education community expressed "serious concern" about the B-minus requirement and "we listened to those concerns and in response to that decided to drop that provision in the HOPE scholarship," Rick Miller, press secretary for Education Secretary Richard Riley, said.
Under the amended proposal, students must show they were making "satisfactory progress" toward graduation and that would be determined by the individual school, Miller said.
The chairman of the House tax-writing committee, where all tax legislation must originate, called it "encouraging" that Clinton took the step to make changes in his proposal.
"It's encouraging to see that President Clinton recognizes the necessity of modifying his educational tax package," House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer said.
"President Clinton today wisely opened up the door to changing his educational provisions," the Texas Republican said in a statement.
The House Ways and Means Committee is expected to start consideration of tax legislation next week.

Another change would eliminate the requirement to subtract the amount of a Pell grant from the HOPE scholarship, Miller said. The Pell grant is an ongoing program that provides a maximum of $2,700 to students each year, with Clinton proposing raising that to $3,000 in fiscal 1998.

"We have made it so that you can receive both the Pell grant and HOPE scholarship together, under the previous proposal you had to deduct the cost of your Pell from your HOPE scholarship," Miller said.
The HOPE scholarship and a proposed $10,000 tuition tax deduction must fit into $35 billion over five years.

Since the changes would allow more people to receive tax relief for higher education and increase the cost of the proposal, there would be some type of a phase-in schedule that had not yet been worked out, Miller said.

"So if we have a $10,000 tax deduction or a $1,500 tax credit, those will not be fully available in the first year," he said. "We'll phase it in until eventually we get to the top dollar number," Miller added.
